title: E.T.: Is It Really the Worst Video Game of All Time?
summary: Josh and Chuck examine the common claim that Atari's 1982 E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial video game is the worst video game of all time. They cover Howard Scott Warshaw's earlier Atari work (Yars' Revenge, Raiders of the Lost Ark), the rushed five-week development schedule set by Atari CEO Ray Kassar after the Steven Spielberg licensing deal, the game's design and glitches, its sales and the returned cartridges, Atari's financial collapse and the 1983 North American video game crash, the urban legend that unsold cartridges were buried in a New Mexico landfill, the 2014 Alamogordo dig featured in the documentary Atari: Game Over, and Warshaw's later life. The episode closes with listener mail about starling droppings and olive oil in Rome.

segments.title: Intro and framing the worst-game claim
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the episode on E.T. being widely called the worst video game of all time, and discuss the 1980s Atari games they played as kids, including Yars' Revenge, Centipede, and Galaga.
topics: worst video game of all time

segments.title: Howard Scott Warshaw and the Raiders game
segments.summary: Warshaw's background: he came to Atari from Hewlett Packard, designed Yars' Revenge, and was known for backstories and Easter eggs. They discuss the difficulty of Raiders of the Lost Ark and the role of kids' imagination in early games.
topics: Raiders of the Lost Ark video game

segments.title: Five-week deadline for E.T.
segments.summary: Ray Kassar called Warshaw to ask whether he could make the E.T. game in five weeks, when such games usually took five to six months. The short schedule came from lengthy licensing negotiations and the Christmas release target. Warshaw agreed and was pitched the game by Steven Spielberg.

segments.title: Building the game and its release
segments.summary: Warshaw worked nearly nonstop for five weeks at home. The game used a six-screen cube-shaped world. Atari had invested about $21 million in the rights and about $5 million in marketing, and the game shipped in time for Christmas.

segments.title: Sales, glitches, and returns
segments.summary: The game sold about a half million copies quickly, then word spread among kids that it was bad. Glitches made E.T. fall into pits repeatedly. Atari had ordered about four million cartridges, and many were returned from stores, leaving millions unsold.

segments.title: Atari's collapse and the 1983 crash
segments.summary: The E.T. failure came as Atari faced competition from personal computers. Atari posted large losses in 1983 and was sold within a year. The North American video game crash cut industry sales sharply, and the blame was placed unfairly on E.T. and Warshaw.

segments.title: Warshaw's later career
segments.summary: Warshaw took time off, worked in real estate, and became a Silicon Valley psychotherapist. He made peace with the reputation of E.T., noting that some who call it the worst game also praise Yars' Revenge.

segments.title: Buried cartridges and the Alamogordo dig
segments.summary: The urban legend that Atari buried unsold E.T. cartridges in a New Mexico landfill was investigated by Mike Burns, with help from former city waste worker Joe Lewandowski, leading to a 2014 excavation documented in Atari: Game Over. Cartridges were found, confirming that some were buried, though not the millions in the legend. Warshaw attended.

segments.title: Cartridge auctions and other bad games
segments.summary: Some recovered cartridges were auctioned on eBay, with the city of Alamogordo getting about $100,000. The hosts note other bad Atari games and that the flood of poor titles may have hurt Atari.

segments.title: Listener mail: starling droppings in Rome
segments.summary: A listener in Rome writes that starlings feeding on olives leave oily droppings that coat cars and make scooter riding slippery.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts sign off and invite listeners to get in touch through the website or email.
